papers.title: When Does Storage Complement Solar? Investment and Cost Recovery under Advanced Net Metering
papers.summary: We examine the joint PV and storage operational and investment decisions of a prosumer under net energy metering (NEM) and peak/off-peak tariffs. Legacy NEM compensates net exports at the retail rate over a netting period, typically under time-invariant pricing. To better reflect system costs, tariff features are being reconsidered, with many U.S. states adopting time-varying prices and export compensation below the retail price. We formulate the prosumer decision problem as a cost minimization problem with charge/discharge, PV investment, and storage investment decisions. We analytically derive the optimal decisions based on the tariff's membership in one of six regions that partition the tariff space. Using these solutions, we examine the relationship between PV and storage, identifying when they are complements or substitutes. Furthermore, we identify the relationship between private DER incentives and the distribution utility's (DU's) net cost of serving the prosumer. For both storage and PV, when investment costs are greater than the costs of serving the customer, there is no tariff where investment in PV and storage decrease non-adopter bills. Under the same conditions, complementarity between PV and storage decreases DU cost recovery for a given tariff. In a Massachusetts-based case study, we validate our theoretical findings by connecting tariff design features to DER interaction, the DU's net cost, and DER adoption in a stochastic, multi-prosumer, and multi-period setting.

papers.title: Finding Competitive Equilibria in Online Marketplaces with Platform Fees, Taxes, and Subsidies
papers.summary: We study equilibrium computation in multi-unit trading networks with valuations satisfying generalized full substitutes and agent- and transaction-specific piecewise-linear transfer functions. These transfers model platform fees, taxes, subsidies, and membership discounts in online marketplaces. Our ascending procedure raises prices at different rates and reaches the minimum equilibrium price vector in finitely many iterations, each implementable in strongly polynomial time under our oracle and arithmetic models. An equilibrium allocation can then be recovered efficiently. The method extends primal-dual techniques developed for ascending auctions to handle complementarities between purchases and sales through a submodular flow formulation. In single-seller markets with substitutes and complements, our framework also extends the double-track auctions of Sun and Yang (2009) and Shioura and Yang (2015) to bidder- and good-specific transfers.

papers.title: Optimal Policy With Noisy Sufficient Statistics
papers.summary: We study how policy-makers should set $k$ policy instruments so as to best hit $m$ (perhaps dynamic) targets, in a linear-quadratic model where there is statistical uncertainty about the causal effects of the policies. Plugging the estimated effects into "sufficient statistics" optimal policy formulas, as commonly done in the literature, can result in infinite risk. In fact, maintaining the status quo regardless of the data is uniquely minimax-optimal when $m>1$, and uniquely minimax-regret-optimal when $m,k>1$. Nevertheless, we recommend that policy-makers adopt a simple, dampened version of the popular plug-in rule, as in Fisher (1962) and Brainard (1967). Not only does this cautious rule outperform doing nothing over most of the parameter space, its worst-case risk is also close to the minimax value in empirically relevant models. Policy-makers should use causal effect estimates from an unbiased but dispersed estimator (such as a local projection) rather than from a moderately biased but precise estimator (such as a vector autoregression).

papers.title: Crowds Believe in You: Online Prediction Markets Overestimate How Often People Achieve Their Own Goals
papers.summary: People increasingly share personal goals online and invite others to forecast them. Research on the planning fallacy finds that observers predict a person's behavior less optimistically than the person does, and prediction markets aggregate such judgments, harnessing the wisdom of crowds. We study 6,150 prediction markets on Manifold in which 1,660 users asked about their own futures ("Will I ...?"), reconstruct every order and execution, and compare these self-markets with markets about external events. Self-markets resolved YES 4.4 percentage points less often than their final prices implied, whereas external markets were nearly calibrated (0.9 points); the difference was 2.2 points at the same price level and 1.9 points within creators who made both kinds of market. Absent when markets opened, the overstatement emerged within a day of trading, even where the person never traded, and peaked in the week before close. In a market's first day, observers moved external-market prices down toward the base rate, but moved self-market prices 3.6 points further toward YES, except in markets naming an outcome the person would not want, which were not overpriced. The correction came late and largely from the person, whose orders supplied 38% of the eventual movement toward the outcome in self-markets, against 9% in external markets. Because self-market prices mainly failed to separate successes from failures, a recalibration learned from earlier markets improved later forecasts by only 1.5%. Crowds believe in the futures people pose for themselves, and the information that would correct them lies with the person.

papers.title: A Proof for Generalized Egalitarianism
papers.summary: This paper proves a rigidity theorem characterizing the Gini-type Lorenz-area ordering under general decision-theoretic constraints together with weak Lorenz dominance, thereby resolving the characterization problem pursued in this line of research on egalitarianism. This does not, of course, bring the broader inquiry to an end. In a certain sense, it may instead mark a step beyond the infancy of our attempt to connect social choice theory, welfare economics, and formal moral philosophy through a common mathematical language. The main proof strategy was originally obtained by the author's own hand, though 5.6sol and Astra could effortlessly reproduce it without any additional hint.

papers.title: Recognizing Dominance through Local Improvement
papers.summary: Strategy-proofness is the traditional standard for predictable behavior, yet participants often fail to play dominant strategies. Most existing simplicity concepts attribute these failures to the cost of contingent reasoning, which they lower by comparing the worst case of the dominant strategy with the best case of an alternative. I argue that there is another approach, one that makes more use of the structure of the strategy set, which I formalize as a neighbor relation. Comparing neighboring strategies can reduce the need for contingent reasoning, and, even with a single contingency, it can simplify the search through the strategy set. I introduce a new simplicity criterion: a mechanism is local improvement solvable under a neighbor relation if repeatedly moving to an improving neighbor always reaches a dominant strategy. Strategy-proofness is the criterion under the coarsest relation, and many classical mechanisms satisfy it under finer ones. In extensive-form mechanisms without duplicate dominant strategies, the criterion under one-situation neighbors is strict action-proofness, which is distinct from obvious strategy-proofness. Among local improvement solvable mechanisms that implement the same outcomes, the criterion predicts more dominant-strategy play where the local comparison is salient.

papers.title: Who Says What: Strategic Communication in Networks
papers.summary: We study a multiplayer communication coordination game in which privately informed agents communicate through a social network and choose their optimal actions while balancing them against their own bliss points and those of their neighbours. We show that equilibrium actions are convex combinations of the expected bliss points of all players, with weights determined by a degree-discounted Bonacich centrality measure. We also characterize when players report truthfully, over-report, or under-report their private information, and show that the incentive to misreport depends critically on the receiver's position in the network. A striking implication is that even under identical preferences, fully revealing communication may not be realized, and information transmission may remain coarse in a star network while becoming almost fully informative in a complete network. Finally, when biases are endogenously chosen, strategic responses to neighbours' biases are governed by their centralities, and unbiasedness may emerge as a Nash equilibrium.

papers.title: Smooth Threshold GARCH: Quasi Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Empirical Evidence
papers.summary: It is well established that the volatility of daily stock returns responds asymmetrically to news, as described by the news impact curve (NIC), which relates volatility to the previous return. Empirical studies suggest that (i) volatility reacts more strongly to negative returns than to positive returns of the same magnitude, (ii) the point of asymmetry, where the NIC attains its minimum, is positive, and (iii) returns above this point often do not increase volatility at all. The popular GJR and A-GARCH models each rule out one of these features. We study the Smooth Threshold GARCH (STGARCH) model, which nests both and allows for (i)-(iii) by combining an estimated threshold, the point of asymmetry, with separate slopes on either side of it. Although the likelihood is not twice continuously differentiable in the threshold, we show that the quasi maximum likelihood estimator is consistent and converges at the usual $\sqrt{n}$-rate, whether or not (iii) holds. If (iii) does not hold, the estimator is asymptotically normal, while if it holds, the slope above the threshold is zero, a value on the boundary of the parameter space, and the limit is non-Gaussian. In that case, the $t$-statistic for (iii) converges to the positive part of a standard normal variable, and the $t$-test of the GJR model remains valid. These results allow us to test the GJR and A-GARCH models, as well as (i)-(iii), within the STGARCH using standard normal critical values. For daily returns on five major stock indices, we reject the GJR model for all five and the A-GARCH model for three, suggesting that the STGARCH improves upon both. Volatility is lowest after returns 0.3-0.6 percentage points above their conditional mean, in line with (i) and (ii). Finally, the hypothesis in (iii) is rejected for two of the five indices.

papers.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
papers.summary: I use AI-assisted replication to assess the empirical importance of negative weights in two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimation, drawing on 1,346 staggered-adoption specifications from 108 economics papers. TWFE estimates are highly correlated with estimates from modern difference-in-differences methods, with observed sign reversals in 10.8-14.5% of comparisons and greater precision for TWFE. Hierarchical models that account for estimation noise imply a 91-98% correlation between estimands and a 0.6-2.1% probability of obtaining a statistically significant TWFE estimate with the opposite sign from the modern estimand. These findings suggest negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice, and illustrate how AI can support large-scale empirical assessments of new econometric methods.

papers.title: Threshold Regression with a Nearly Integrated Threshold Variable
papers.summary: This paper considers threshold regression with an integrated or local-to-unity threshold variable and a threshold fixed in levels. We study the least squares threshold estimator and establish its asymptotic theory under both fixed and diminishing threshold effects. Under a fixed effect, the threshold estimator has a compound Cox argmin limit, whereas under a diminishing effect, its limiting distribution is characterized by a two-sided Brownian argmax with a random scale. We also develop likelihood ratio inference, which is asymptotically pivotal under a diminishing effect and conservative under Gaussian errors for a fixed effect, and show that conventional $t$-ratios for the slope coefficients remain asymptotically standard normal. A sup-Wald test is proposed to detect threshold effects that may be too small for consistent threshold localization. We further extend the framework to allow for integrated slope regressors and for contemporaneous endogeneity of the threshold variable, showing that the leading endogenous contribution cancels over shrinking threshold windows. Monte Carlo simulations examine the finite-sample performance of the proposed methods. An illustration using public debt and economic growth highlights the relevance of allowing for a persistent threshold variable.

papers.title: When are complements and substitutes dual?
papers.summary: For binary-action games on bipartite networks, strategic complements and strategic substitutes are one and the same: each can be transformed into the other by relabelling the actions of every player on exactly one side. In this note, I show that bipartiteness is necessary and sufficient for such a relabelling; as a consequence, bipartite networks are precisely those on which every binary-action game with strategic substitutes must have a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

papers.title: Did the energy crisis turn borrowers green? Zonal power prices and green bond choice on Oslo Børs
papers.summary: The energy crisis of 2021 to 2023 caused a sharp increase in Nordic electricity prices, with substantial differences across bidding zones. We use this variation to examine whether issuers exposed to higher local electricity prices were more likely to choose green bonds over conventional bonds. We construct a dataset of bonds listed on Oslo Børs between 2019 and 2025 by combining ESMA FIRDS reference data, including matured bonds, with Euronext green bond classifications and issuer registry information. We then match issuers to their electricity bidding zones and examine the relationship between local power prices and green bond choice using issuer and quarter fixed effects. The share of green bonds among new listings increased from 15% in 2019 to 48% in 2024, but we find no statistically significant evidence that higher local electricity prices increased the likelihood of green bond issuance. This finding is consistent across price exposure windows of three to twelve months and for both utilities and other issuers. However, the estimates rely on 21 identifying issuers, and the minimum detectable effect at 80% statistical power is 3.1 percentage points for a 10 EUR/MWh increase in electricity prices, meaning that smaller effects cannot be ruled out. The estimated effect is larger but imprecise among issuers with an earlier green bond, which implies an existing framework. We also find no clear association between carbon prices and green bond choice, although this analysis covers only eight utilities. Overall, the findings suggest that the growth of green bond issuance in Norway was more closely associated with broader market trends than with differences in local electricity prices.

papers.title: What is Work For? Labor, Politics, and Meaning in the Age of AI
papers.summary: This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original "Work Values" Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job--valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI transition, understanding attitudes to AI, and making sense of policy preferences. Guaranteeing a basic income may indeed be necessary for managing any future AI labor shock, yet it could ultimately fail to compensate workers for any loss of the non-monetary benefits they derive from work.

papers.title: Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
papers.summary: Classical theory predicts that irrational traders lose money to rational traders and are eventually driven out of the market. Yet noise trading, herding, and heuristic trading persist even in highly developed markets. We model a financial market as an ecology of two trading-behavior types, relatively rational (R) and boundedly rational (N), whose composition evolves under replicator dynamics according to relative performance. Each type's fitness depends on the share of the other type and on frictions. When the interaction is complementary, that is, rational traders profit from the mispricing created by boundedly rational traders while the latter benefit from the liquidity and price correction supplied by the former, and when the difference in frictions is moderate, a unique interior composition exists and is globally asymptotically stable: bounded rationality persists endogenously. When the interaction is antagonistic, the same point becomes a tipping threshold between two one-type regimes. Comparative statics show that lowering the costs of disciplined trading, as algorithmic and AI-based trading does, shifts the composition toward rational trading continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless the cost advantage exceeds an explicit threshold.

papers.title: The Welfare Limits of Market Segmentation with Captive Consumers
papers.summary: In a duopoly with captive and contested consumers, I characterize every pair of consumer and producer surplus that can arise under some market composition and some public segmentation, and construct a market that produces each pair. The set is lens-shaped. At any level of industry profit, consumers do worst when captive and contested consumers are perfectly separated and best in an unsegmented market in which the two firms have equally many captives. A market with unequal captive bases and some contested consumers cannot reach this upper frontier under any segmentation. Between Bertrand competition and monopoly, the frontier itself lies strictly below what consumers would get if everyone paid a single deterministic price yielding the same profit. Firms must randomize, and with downward-sloping demand the resulting price dispersion lowers consumer surplus.

papers.title: Measuring Longer-Horizon Leveraged ETF Performance
papers.summary: Many investors hold leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs) for more than one day. Because these products reset leverage daily, their longer-horizon returns need not equal the stated leverage multiple times the underlying return. We explain this gap using a return identity that separates what we call the convexity bonus, volatility drag, and product costs. We also discuss several common ways to measure LETF performance and highlight how these measures can produce misleading assessments of how real-world LETFs perform. We propose evaluating ex-post performance using realized terminal wealth, which measures how much invested wealth grew. For ex-ante analysis, we propose using expected log returns to quantify how fast capital compounds over time. We show that estimating expected cumulative return by compounding the historical arithmetic mean can rank investments backwards, report gains for funds that lose money, suggest that infinite leverage is optimal when expected returns exceed borrowing cost, and reward temporary price fluctuations that reduce LETF wealth. We argue that even if the distribution of daily returns is known by the econometrician, expected terminal wealth is sensitive to whether the model draws days independently or draws monthly or annual blocks of daily returns and can be driven by a small number of economically infeasible payouts.

papers.title: Capital growth since the 19th century
papers.summary: We argued in an earlier paper (Getty and Tkachenko 2025b), from data reported for net saving and market-value capital by 94 nations over the period 1980-2021, that net saving has had little or no effect on capital growth at the global scale. Here we extend the study backward to the earliest year, in each country, for which those data have been reported or reconstructed. We find a still smaller margin of possibility (1.6% versus 6.4%) of contribution of net saving to capital growth at the collective scale. We also propose and defend an alternative explanation of capital growth, and suggest a larger role for the cash flow concept in economic analysis.

papers.title: Orthogonal Inference for Conditional Z-Estimation without Cross-Fitting: A Distributional Nearest-Neighbor Approach
papers.summary: Estimating conditional parameters, such as heterogeneous treatment effects, often requires rich covariate adjustment, even when the parameters are reported along only a few dimensions. Fitting nuisance functions on the full sample makes all observations available for adjustment, but creates dependence between fitted scores and the observations at which they are evaluated, which is typically avoided by cross-fitting. We develop pointwise inference with full-sample nuisance predictions for exactly identified conditional moment equations, recovering conditional average treatment effects as a special case. We localize the estimating equations around the reporting point using distributional nearest neighbors (DNN), a U-statistic-based averaging procedure. Under sufficient conditions on the local design, orthogonality, prediction accuracy and quantitative deletion stability, the estimator is asymptotically normal, and a frozen-score jackknife consistently estimates its limiting covariance with nuisance predictions held fixed. In simulations, full-sample and cross-fitted inference perform similarly, with coverage shortfalls from nuisance approximation error, spatial bias and heavy studentized tails. An application to 401(k) eligibility using Survey of Income and Program Participation data finds similar estimates across nuisance prediction methods, with wide normal-reference intervals.

papers.title: The Hidden Value of Soft Infrastructure for Urban Flood Adaptation
papers.summary: As sea level rises and flooding events become more frequent, cities are tapping into a range of engineering and planning solutions to reduce flood losses. Beyond traditional ``hard'' infrastructure (e.g., sewage, seawalls), ``soft'' infrastructure that supports and empowers the role of citizens in preparedness has been hailed as a promising avenue for improving adaptation. Despite its promise, there have been very limited attempts to quantify its effectiveness in reducing losses relative to hard infrastructure, particularly in urban environments. This study fills this knowledge gap using generative AI to quantify the effectiveness of a range of hard and soft infrastructure in urban areas. We demonstrate, for the first time, that soft infrastructure can significantly reduce flood losses, with an impact on par with hard infrastructure. Our results open the door to novel ways of confronting adaptation challenges in cities. Soft infrastructure is a viable alternative, especially when budgetary or time constraints make hard infrastructure unattainable. Policymakers should also couple soft and hard infrastructure to maximize resilience.

papers.title: Can Artificial Intelligence Forecast Treatment Effects in Economics?
papers.summary: I use LLMs to forecast treatment effects of research studies pre-registered on the AEA RCT Registry and the Open Science Framework. I focus on studies whose results were first publicly released in 2026 and elicit forecasts from models whose training or knowledge cut-off dates were before the relevant set of papers was released. First, LLM models extract forecasting questions from the pre-registrations or pre-analysis plans. These questions elicit forecasted treatment effects; not all resolve in the subsequent papers, but those that do can be used to consider forecast accuracy. Forecasts were elicited for 889 treatment effects from 39 papers with results disclosed in January 2026 or later, or 673 from 33 papers after screening. Forecasts were elicited in raw units but I focus on those that could be standardized and therefore compared across papers. Currently, the median absolute forecast error is 0.054 SD for the best model, the average absolute error is 0.093 SD, and the MSE is 0.0218. The AI forecasts perform substantially better than benchmarks forecasting 0 effect or forecasting the mean effect of other papers' results in that time period. Overall, these results suggest considerable scope for forecasts to be of value in informing policy and research.

papers.title: The existence of anonymous, stationary, monotone social welfare functions satisfying restricted dominance: an answer to an open question in intergenerational equity
papers.summary: In this note, we consider social welfare functions on infinite utility streams and answer an open question posed in Asheim et al. (2021, Remark 1). There exists a real-valued representation of social welfare preferences that satisfies monotonicity, stationarity, restricted dominance, and strong anonymity, hence also finite anonymity. Our social welfare function satisfies a stronger finite-rank sensitivity condition, Liminf-Restricted Dominance, in the sense of Asheim et al. (2022) and Asheim et al. (2025). Our construction shows that limited discontinuity is not redundant in Asheim et al. (2021, Proposition 2): once that diagonal continuity condition is dropped, even arbitrary-permutation invariance can coexist with stationarity and non-trivial sensitivity.
papers.journal_ref: Economics Bulletin, Volume 46, Issue 3, Year 2026, pages 1007-1013

papers.title: Quantile Methods in Large Panels with Fixed Effects
papers.summary: We study quantile regression (QR) and instrumental variable quantile regression (QIV) in static panel data models with additive individual fixed effects. We derive the asymptotic distribution of the fixed effects estimator as both panel dimensions grow large, showing that it has an asymptotic bias of order 1/T, where T is the number of observations per individual. The bias analysis relies on a novel characterization of the profiled score as a weighted sum of induced order statistics (concomitants), which yields an exact finite-T expression for the score bias. We propose Jackknife bias corrections and uncover a bias-variance tradeoff that is specific to the non-smooth quantile objective functions. The standard delete-one Jackknife fails to eliminate the leading bias and, even when modified to achieve bias correction, inflates the variance so that only $\sqrt{N}$-consistency is attained, where N is the number of individuals. We propose a modified Jackknife bias correction for general subsample sizes, derive the asymptotic distribution of the resulting estimator, and show that $\sqrt{NT}$-consistency and valid inference are achieved for suitable choices of the subsample size. As an empirical application, we study the effect of age on school children's test scores using school fixed effects.

papers.title: Debiasing Functionals of Conditional Distributions
papers.summary: Many economic parameters depend on estimated conditional distributions. We construct locally robust moments for these parameters by representing their first-step derivative and centering the representer conditionally on the covariates. We develop complementary conditional-measure and CDF linearizations, and derive corrections for control functions, counterfactual functionals, conditional rank-rank regression, and transformations of conditional $L$-functionals. Under the CDF linearization, a Riesz-regression criterion estimates the correction automatically; its analysis distinguishes representer estimation from integration against the estimated conditional law. We establish asymptotic oracle equivalence, asymptotic normality, and consistent variance estimation for cross-fitted estimators under continuity and remainder conditions, without requiring functional weak convergence of the first-step estimators. An exact linear representation yields double robustness; for rank-rank regression this property is componentwise. Simulations report reductions in bias and RMSE relative to plug-in estimation, with double cross-fitting improving the finite-sample performance.

papers.title: Simultaneous Gradient Learning in First-Price Auctions
papers.summary: We study equilibrium learning in discretized Bayesian games, focusing on first-price auctions as a testbed for gradient-based learning dynamics under private information. While the symmetric independent private values model admits a unique Bayesian correlated equilibrium (BCE) in the continuous limit, standard convergence guarantees for gradient-based learners do not apply: classical no-regret theory predicts convergence only to Bayesian coarse correlated equilibria (BCCE), which can remain large and far from the competitive equilibrium even under fine discretizations. To bridge this gap, we introduce the notion of Bayesian semicoarse correlated equilibrium (BSCCE), an equilibrium concept that refines BCCE by restricting deviations to probability-preserving transformations consistent with projected gradient dynamics. We provide a linear programming characterization of BSCCE with polynomially many variables and constraints and establish the inclusion hierarchy $BCE \subseteq BSCCE \subseteq BCCE$. Our main finding is that the BSCCE set contracts in many cases as the discretization of the Bayesian game is refined. Even with priors for which BCCE fails to concentrate, the diameter of the BSCCE polytope shrinks toward zero, indicating convergence to the unique continuous-game Bayes-Nash equilibrium. These results provide a principled explanation for the observed robustness of gradient-based learning in discretized Bayesian games, showing that these dynamics select a smaller equilibrium set than standard no-regret theory predicts.

papers.title: Pawnshops and Property-Related Crime: Lessons from Interwar Tokyo
papers.summary: Using ward-level panel data for 1927 to 1935 and fixed-effects models, this study examines how pawnshops were related to property-related crime in interwar Tokyo. Accordingly, public pawnshops targeting low-income borrowers are compared with profit-oriented private pawnshops. The results reveal that public lending is negatively associated with theft and positively associated with fraud and extortion, whereas private lending is negatively associated with fraud and extortion as well as embezzlement. A simple monetization exercise shows that offense counts and victim losses can yield different assessments. Overall, the relationship between credit and crime depended on both institutional design and crime type.

papers.title: When an effort-maximizing team architecture is unstable
papers.summary: Organizations choose team structures to intensify competition, yet their members may prefer to reorganize. We ask whether an architecture that maximizes aggregate effort can remain stable when contestants may form a replacement team from incumbent rosters. When a coalition draws from identical teams and reproduces their type, its members and the designer rank the reorganization in opposite directions: the coalition gains precisely when total effort falls. A strict effort optimum can therefore supply its own blocking certificate, while a stable optimum can survive only on a plateau where every reachable reorganization of this kind leaves effort unchanged. In a linear benchmark, we characterize stability against every feasible one-team reorganization and global effort maximization over every feasible partition. Except under pair capacity, the two regions do not overlap; with pair capacity, they meet only at one boundary. The ordering persists in a matched quadratic benchmark with strictly convex effort cost, and broader one-step deviation rights cannot restore overlap. Among standardized full-cap designs, the unique stable-effort optimum uses the largest feasible roster and sets incentive concentration at its blocking boundary.

papers.title: Optimal Information Disclosure in Classic Auctions Revisited: Endogenous Information Acquisition and Costly Verification
papers.summary: We revisit the influential distribution-independent optimal disclosure result of Bergemann, Heumann, Morris, Sorokin, and Winter (2022), whose optimal disclosure policy reveals low bidder values and pools high values at a critical quantile depending only on the number of bidders, and show that this policy is no longer generally revenue-maximizing even for the familiar uniform and binary valuation distributions, once bidders can endogenously acquire private information through costly verification. The underlying reason reflects a fundamental principle of incentive-based mechanism design, rooted in Hurwicz's analysis of structural invariance and echoed in the Lucas critique: economic agents respond strategically to changes in the information and incentives they face. This is the essence of \emph{trust, but verify}. A change in disclosure policy may leave the underlying economic primitives unchanged while altering bidders' verification decisions and the resulting equilibrium information structure. We establish existence and uniqueness of the symmetric Bayesian Nash verification equilibrium, characterize equilibrium-implementable disclosure policies, and derive an exact revenue decomposition and a general characterization of global optimality. We further develop optimality conditions and structural results that provide a systematic foundation for analyzing optimal disclosure with endogenous information acquisition.

papers.title: How to Pick a Model if You Must
papers.summary: I axiomatize Berk-Nash equilibrium in decision problems with possibly misspecified models. I specify how a rule--which selects a set of action-belief pairs in a problem--ought to compare a correct forecast with an incorrect one, react to the removal of models, and accommodate additional observations that do not distinguish among the models. Together with axioms concerning attitudes toward randomization and payoffs, and a pair of regularity conditions, these axioms characterize Berk-Nash equilibrium.

papers.title: A Sequential Foundation for Two-Level Nested Logit
papers.summary: I show that the two-level nested logit demand model arises exactly from a sequential choice process in which group, subgroup, and product taste shocks are revealed stage by stage. The result extends to any number of levels and holds for any nesting parameters below one, without the bounds and ordering that random utility maximization requires. Estimates that applied work discards for violating these bounds are therefore consistent with sequential choice. The standard linear inversion and welfare formula remain valid. Adding a product to a nest can raise another product's share in that nest, even with single-unit demand.

papers.title: fastC-GC and fastC-GC*: Efficient RCCP-Guided Graph Estimation for Time Series
papers.summary: We introduce fastC-GC and fastC-GC$^*$, computationally efficient methods for time-series graph estimation using the two-test rule motivated by Reichenbach's common cause principle (RCCP) and the conditioning sets of causalised Granger causality (c-GC and c-GC$^*$). The methods use standardized data, ridge-residual correlation, and complete circular shift enumeration evaluated by Fourier transforms. Shared precision calculations and Schur downdates avoid repeated regression fits. On a single-threaded benchmark, fastC-GC was 68-277 times faster than the compared c-GC implementation, and fastC-GC$^*$ was 192-886 times faster than c-GC$^*$. Across four suites with reference graphs, aggregate mean area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) differed from the corresponding baseline by at most 0.019, but F1 was lower at the selected thresholds in every suite. The computational gains therefore accompany a change in estimator and selected graphs. Among eight methods, Bagged PCMCI+ had the highest mean AUPRC on sparse VAR, an autocorrelated structural process, and DREAM3; CUTS+ led on Lorenz-96. Wind-tunnel and river-discharge applications illustrate differences between inferred graphs without establishing causal accuracy. We prove the computational identities and a restricted population adjacency result for fastC-GC$^*$. Causal interpretation requires the stated graphical assumptions; validity of the implemented tests additionally requires a suitable shift-invariant null law. Empirical null rejection rates informed the conditional threshold $β= 0.005$, without establishing general test validity or graph-wide error control.

papers.title: Contemporaneous Transmission Networks and Systemic Risk in European Banking
papers.summary: We study how contemporaneous equity-return transmission shapes systemic exposure among 51 listed European banks. Using a recursive non-Gaussian network model on volatility-standardized returns, we construct two market-capitalization-weighted measures based on direct and indirect transmission effects: the Systemic Impact Score (SIS), capturing a bank's potential influence on other institutions, and the Systemic Vulnerability Score (SVS), capturing its exposure to disturbances originating elsewhere. The fitted network reveals distinct transmitting and receiving roles, highlighting differences between institutions with substantial outward influence and those with high incoming sensitivity. Receiving roles are generally more reproducible than transmitting roles across repeated network discovery, and selected connections remain informative about lower-tail dependence in subsequent observations. Volatility standardization substantially reduces detected dependence among recovered shocks, although the full-sample model does not satisfy the designated criterion for supporting shock independence. Alternative recursive orderings also yield comparable directional tail asymmetries, limiting the extent to which these patterns validate a particular ordering. The results provide complementary measures of model-implied systemic transmission and vulnerability, with explicit attention to uncertainty and identification limits

papers.title: Hosting is not capturing: an exposure-capability framework and Hungary's electric-vehicle battery bet
papers.summary: How should a dependent economy respond when a polycrisis turns economic integration from a source of efficiency into a surface of vulnerability? This paper develops the exposure-capability framework, which maps a country's strategic options along two dimensions - the concentration of its external dependence and the depth of its productive capability - and yields four ideal strategies. It applies the framework to Hungary's large-scale bet on electric-vehicle battery manufacturing, asking what the concentrated exposure purchased: movement toward a higher position in the battery value chain, as a catch-up gamble, or the reproduction of the country's existing position under a new product, as dependent entrenchment. Using a firm-level panel of Hungary's largest companies for 2010-2024, it tests four hypotheses and examines the conditions attached to the support that financed the investments. The sector has expanded enormously, but its value capture neither rises beyond the recovery from construction losses nor shifts up the chain: production remains concentrated in the lowest-value stage, matures only to the level of comparably young foreign-owned firms, and does not cover its own costs. The support that financed it required investment volume, revenue and employment retention; capability-relevant criteria entered the decree as considerations rather than conditions, and a capability-contingent instrument within the same scheme went unused. On the evidence to 2024 the bet is a lateral substitution at constant quality, in which battery-cell fabrication replaces automotive assembly at the same dependent position. Hosting the green transition's supply chain, the case shows, is not the same as capturing its value.

papers.title: Climate change, sea level rise, and the agricultural revolution
papers.summary: We test various hypotheses for the invention and spread of agriculture: higher temperatures, increased seasonality, carbon dioxide fertilization, sea level rise, and technological progress on the extensive margin. We successfully replicate Matranga (QJE 2024). His seasonality hypothesis survives alternative data, estimators, and competing hypotheses. Population density played a role in the invention of agriculture, while spatial diffusion was important for its spread. Sea level rise and climate change had a minor effect on the population density of the areas that first adopted agriculture. Extrapolating a logit model for the invention of agriculture, some now-submerged areas in the Persian Gulf, Mediterranean, and Yellow Sea were suitable for early agriculture. Over time, technological progress was the main factor in extending agriculture's extensive margin.

papers.title: Personal preference or system role? Battery swapping among UK electric vehicle users
papers.summary: Battery swapping replaces a depleted EV battery with a charged one, reducing waiting time and enabling off-peak charging. Evidence on acceptance, however, remains concentrated in Asian markets, and most studies examine individual adoption intentions. This study asks whether current UK EV users judge swapping differently as a purchase option and as a technology for the transport system. Using Behavioural Reasoning Theory, an integrated choice and latent variable model, and latent class analysis, we analyse perceived usefulness, energy-system concerns, practical barriers, and satisfaction with current charging. Usefulness and energy-system concerns relate more strongly to expectations about the system. Battery compatibility and station coverage relate more strongly to personal preference, while spare battery costs relate to expectations about network viability. User groups differ in how they balance benefits, barriers, and satisfaction with existing charging. Policy should address driver barriers and network viability as distinct but connected priorities.

papers.title: Identifying and disentangling direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
papers.summary: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.
